summary: An April Fools' RFC that takes a humorous look at the tangle of three letter acronyms. It pretends to give IANA considerations so that one acronym does not have several expansions. It is not a real standard and should be read as a joke.

eli5.summary: Many different things share the same three-letter nickname, which causes mix-ups. This joke note pretends to sort them all out with serious-sounding rules, but it is really just for fun.

questions: is there an april fools rfc about acronyms
what is the rfc about tlas
subtitle: A humorous RFC about managing the world's supply of three-letter acronyms

tldr.problem: The Internet community has used so many Three-Letter Acronyms (TLAs) that the same acronym has multiple meanings. TCP might mean "Transmission Control Protocol" or (in the RFC) "Totally Bad Proposal." This RFC jokingly warns that TLAs are running out and proposes serious-sounding solutions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5513, published on April 1st, proposes that IANA create an "Internet TLA Registry" (helpfully, a Badly Construed Proposal or BCP) with rules for allocating TLAs. It reserves certain TLAs with humorous alternative meanings and defines allocation policies, all presented in grave technical language despite the joke.
tldr.outcome: A lighthearted exploration of how deeply three-letter acronyms have burrowed into Internet culture, poking fun at registry processes while being technically accurate about the problem of acronym collision.

today: RFC 5513 is an April Fools' joke and not a real standard. It remains a humorous commentary on the role of acronyms in Internet culture and the genuine problem of acronym collision.

sections.title: A Serious Problem, Presented As Humor
sections.content:
This RFC is an April Fools' Day joke. RFC 5513 takes a real problem (acronym collision and overuse) and proposes an absurdly bureaucratic solution with exaggerated gravity. The author notes that acronyms are valued not for their merit but for their presence: a protocol with 20 TLAs is considered more successful than one with 12. The RFC cites TCP as having "no fewer than 20 distinct TLAs" (though "some are simple abbreviations rather than proper acronyms") and suggests this abundance is why TCP is successful while the Internet Stream Protocol (variously ST2 or STII) has been less successful.

The joke premise is that the Internet is rapidly approaching World Acronym Depletion (WAD), calculated to occur by the end of September in the RFC's April 1st publication year.
sections.eli5: This whole document is a joke written on April 1st. It seriously proposes rationing three-letter nicknames like they're a scarce metal, even calculating when we'd run out if the joke were real.

sections.title: The Proposed TLA Registry (Not Real)
sections.content:
The RFC proposes that IANA create an Internet TLA Registry (helpfully, a Badly Construed Proposal, or BCP). It reserves certain acronyms with humorous alternative definitions: TLA means Two Letter Acronym, RFC means Ready for Compost, BCP means Badly Construed Proposal, and VPN means Very Possibly No Use.

The allocation policies are presented in bureaucratic deadpan: Experimental TLAs (form starting with XX), First Come First Served (starting with X, Y, or Z), and IETF Review (everything else). The document even includes a humorous conversation between two people about ST2 (Internet Streams) that plays on the ambiguity.
sections.eli5: The joke creates a pretend list where common words get silly meanings for fun. It then divvies up which new three-letter nicknames would be easy to grab and which need permission.

sections.title: What the Joke Reveals About Real Problems
sections.content:
Despite the humor, RFC 5513 touches real issues: acronym overload makes technical documentation hard to follow, many acronyms are ambiguous, and the IETF has long used acronyms as a badge of technical complexity. The RFC notes that security algorithms are identified by acronyms, so an engineer implementing MD5 must know whether it means the real message digest algorithm or one of the many conflicting alternative definitions.

The backward compatibility section jokes about Solomon's judgment: if an acronym has three uses, each use gets one letter, etc. The document is technically accurate in its descriptions of the problem, funny in its proposed solution.
sections.eli5: The joke actually points out something real: it is genuinely hard to know what people mean when they use three-letter nicknames because so many things share them. Knowing which MD5 someone means (the real one, or a joke version) matters for security.
